title: How Jews Read: Parashah, Midrash, Commentary
bigQuestion: How does Jewish tradition read the Tanakh, and why does it treat arguing about a verse as a way of honoring it?

story.title: A Page Full of Voices
story.kicker: One verse sits in the middle of the page, and around it, in smaller type, readers from five centuries take turns talking back.
paragraphs: A seventh grader named Maya opens a heavy book in her synagogue library. She is looking for Genesis 1:1, and she finds it, but it is only a few lines in the middle of a big page. The verse is in large Hebrew letters. Everything else on the page is small print wrapped around it, like a crowd around a speaker.

Her teacher shows her how to read it. Just under the verse is an Aramaic translation, the Targum, from roughly the 2nd century CE. In the inner margin is Rashi, a rabbi who lived in France in the 11th century. His first comment asks a question: why does the Torah start with creation instead of with the first commandment?

Down the outer margin is Ibn Ezra, a Spanish scholar from the 12th century. He cares about grammar and sometimes disagrees with Rashi. Below him is Ramban, from 13th-century Spain. He argues with both of them. Near the bottom is a later commentator quoting a midrash, a rabbinic story. It asks what existed before the world was made.

Maya notices something. None of these readers erases the one before. They pile up. A reader in 1270 answers a reader in 1100, who answered a reader in 200, and the verse stays in the middle, unchanged. The book is called *Mikraot Gedolot*, the Great Scriptures, and it was first printed in Venice in the 1520s.

This chapter is about that page. It is about how Jewish communities read the Tanakh. They read it in a yearly cycle, out loud and together. They fill the story's gaps with midrash. They speak of layers of meaning. And they keep commentators who argue across the centuries. In Jewish tradition, to argue with a text carefully is to take it seriously.
story.think: Why might a community keep printing old disagreements beside a verse instead of printing just one correct explanation?

lessons.title: The Weekly Portion
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah is divided into 54 portions, one read each Shabbat, so the whole Torah is read aloud in a year and begun again on Simchat Torah.
reading: Every Saturday morning, in synagogues around the world, the same part of the Torah is read aloud. That part is called the *parashah*, the portion. The Torah is divided into 54 portions. Read one a week, with some weeks doubled up, and the whole Torah is finished in a year.

Each portion is named for one of its first words. The first is Bereshit, "in the beginning." The portion about Noah is called Noach. The one where Abraham is told to leave home is Lekh Lekha, "go forth." Many Jews know the year by its portions. Others know it by months.

The cycle ends and begins on one day. On the holiday of *Simchat Torah*, "rejoicing in the Torah," the reader chants the last lines of Deuteronomy, where Moses dies. Then, without a pause, another reader begins Genesis 1. The scrolls are carried around the synagogue with singing and dancing.

Historians note that this yearly cycle was the custom of Babylonian Jews. Jews in the land of Israel once used a cycle of about three years. The Babylonian custom won out by the Middle Ages, and today nearly every community follows the one-year cycle.

words.d: the weekly Torah portion; there are 54, read in a yearly cycle
"rejoicing in the Torah"; the holiday when the yearly reading ends with Deuteronomy and begins again with Genesis

look.title: Weekly Portions in Each Book of the Torah
look.cite: Standard division of the Torah into 54 parashot, as printed in Hebrew Bibles and Jewish calendars
look.prompt: A year has 52 weeks, and some of them are holidays. How does a community fit 54 portions into one year?

check.q: What is a parashah?
choices: A margin note by the Masoretes
The weekly Torah portion read on Shabbat
A short book among the Writings
The reading from the Prophets
check.why: Parashah means portion; the Torah is split into 54 of them so it is read through in a year.

check.q: What happens on Simchat Torah?
choices: The scroll is buried in a cemetery
The book of Esther is read with noisemakers
The reading of Deuteronomy ends and Genesis begins again the same day
The Torah is read in Aramaic
check.why: Simchat Torah closes the yearly cycle with the last verses of Deuteronomy and opens it again with Genesis 1.

check.q: How are the weekly portions named?
choices: For the rabbi who first read them
By number, from 1 to 54
For the holiday nearest to them
For one of their first words
check.why: Each portion takes its name from an opening word, such as Bereshit, Noach or Lekh Lekha.

lessons.title: A Reading from the Prophets
lessons.mainIdea: After the Torah portion, a passage from the Prophets called the haftarah is chanted, chosen to echo the portion or the holiday.
reading: The Torah reading is not the last reading of the morning. After it comes the *haftarah*, a passage from the Nevi'im, the Prophets. The word means something like conclusion or dismissal. It is usually a chapter or so, chanted to its own melody.

Each haftarah is matched to its week. When the Torah portion tells of Noah and the flood, the haftarah is from Isaiah 54. That chapter mentions "the waters of Noah." When the portion describes the building of the Mishkan, the desert sanctuary, the haftarah tells of Solomon building the Temple. On holidays the haftarah fits the day instead.

No one knows for sure when the custom began. It is already assumed in the Mishnah, around 200 CE, so it is old. A later story says it started when a foreign king banned Torah reading and Jews read the Prophets instead. Historians treat that story as a guess, not a fact.

The haftarah does something important for the shape of the Tanakh. Most of the Prophets are never read from a scroll in a yearly cycle the way the Torah is. The haftarah is where the synagogue hears Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Amos and Hosea, a piece at a time, all year long.

words.d: the reading from the Prophets chanted after the Torah portion on Shabbat and holidays
the portable sanctuary the Torah says the Israelites built in the wilderness; also called the tabernacle

look.title: Matching a Prophet to a Portion
look.text: The Torah portion Noach tells how the world was flooded and how God promised never to flood it again. Its haftarah, Isaiah 54:9–10 in JPS 1917, has God say that just as He swore the waters of Noah would never again cover the earth, so He swears not to be angry with Israel, and that the mountains may move but His kindness will not.
look.prompt: What word or image links the two passages? Why might the people who chose this haftarah want listeners to hear the flood story and Isaiah's promise on the same morning?

check.q: From which part of the Tanakh is the haftarah taken?
choices: The Prophets (Nevi'im)
The Torah
The Writings (Ketuvim)
The Talmud
check.why: The haftarah is a passage from the Prophets, chosen to fit the Torah portion or the holiday.

check.q: How is a haftarah chosen for a regular Shabbat?
choices: It is the next chapter after last week's haftarah
It echoes a theme or image in that week's Torah portion
The rabbi picks any passage
It is always from the book of Isaiah
check.why: For example, the portion about Noah is paired with Isaiah 54, which mentions the waters of Noah.

check.q: What do historians say about the story that the haftarah began during a ban on Torah reading?
choices: It is proven by the Dead Sea Scrolls
It is recorded in the book of Esther
It is a later guess, not an established fact
It was invented by Rashi
check.why: The custom is already assumed in the Mishnah, but its origin is unknown; the ban story is a later explanation without evidence.

lessons.title: Reading Together
lessons.mainIdea: The Torah is read in community: a quorum of ten, members called up in turn, and young people reading for the first time at a bar or bat mitzvah.
reading: In Jewish practice, the Torah is read out loud in a group, not silently alone. A public reading needs a *minyan*, a quorum of ten adult Jews. In some communities, that means ten men. In many others today, women count too. Without a minyan, the scroll stays in the ark.

The reading is split into sections, and for each one a member is called up to the scroll. Being called up is an *aliyah*, from a word meaning going up. On Shabbat morning there are seven aliyot. The person called says a blessing, the reader chants, and the person says a closing blessing. It is an honor, and it is shared around.

A young person who reads from the Torah for the first time is marking a *bar mitzvah* or *bat mitzvah*, son or daughter of the commandment. Jewish tradition sets the age at thirteen for boys. For girls it is twelve in some communities and thirteen in others. The first bat mitzvah in the United States was Judith Kaplan's, in New York in 1922.

Why read together? One answer from Jewish tradition is that the Torah was given to a whole people at Sinai, not to one person. Another is practical: a listener follows the reader and catches any slip, so the community, not just the reader, guards the text. Many Chicago synagogues also teach the reading to adults who never learned it as children.

words.d: a quorum of ten adult Jews needed for a public Torah reading and certain prayers
"going up"; being called to the Torah scroll to say the blessings for a section of the reading
"son or daughter of the commandment"; a Jewish young person who has reached the age of religious responsibility, often marked by reading Torah

look.title: Numbers in a Shabbat Torah Service
look.cite: Mishnah Megillah 4:2–3 for the quorum and the number of readers; Judith Kaplan's bat mitzvah, New York, 1922
look.prompt: Why might a tradition require ten people before a scroll may be read? What does a minimum number say about the kind of reading it is?

check.q: What is a minyan?
choices: The pointer used to follow the text
The seven readings on Shabbat
The room where the scrolls are stored
A quorum of ten adult Jews needed for a public Torah reading
check.why: A minyan is the ten-person quorum; without it the Torah is not read publicly.

check.q: What does it mean to have an aliyah?
choices: To be called up to the Torah to say blessings for a section
To move to Jerusalem
To chant the haftarah in Aramaic
To buy a new scroll for the synagogue
check.why: Aliyah means going up; in the synagogue it is the honor of being called to the scroll during the reading.

check.q: At what age does Jewish tradition say a boy becomes a bar mitzvah?
check.why: A boy becomes bar mitzvah at thirteen; a girl becomes bat mitzvah at twelve or thirteen, depending on the community.

lessons.title: What Midrash Is
lessons.mainIdea: Midrash is the rabbis' way of searching a text, filling its gaps with stories and explanations that grow out of its words.
reading: The Tanakh leaves a lot out. It does not say what Isaac thought on the way up the mountain. It does not say why God chose Abraham. Jewish readers noticed these gaps early, and they answered them with *midrash*. The word comes from a root meaning to search or to seek. A midrash is what you find when you search a verse hard.

Midrash is not free invention. It starts from something in the text: an odd word, a repeated phrase, a detail that seems out of place. The rabbis asked why that detail was there. Their answers often took the form of a story. Those stories were collected in books such as Genesis Rabbah, edited around the 5th century CE.

There are two broad kinds. Midrash *halakhah* searches the Torah for law: how exactly to keep Shabbat, or what counts as fair weights in a market. Midrash *aggadah* searches for story and meaning: what Sarah said, what the angels argued about, why the letter bet begins the Torah. This chapter mostly deals with aggadah.

Jewish tradition does not treat every midrash as history. Rabbis often gave several midrashim on one verse, some of them contradicting each other. The point was to open the text, not to close it. A student who learns a midrash learns one way that readers long ago heard a verse.

words.d: rabbinic searching of a text; a story or explanation that grows from a word, gap or oddity in a verse (plural: midrashim)
the story-and-meaning side of rabbinic teaching, as opposed to law
Jewish law; the way of walking; midrash halakhah draws law from the Torah's words

look.title: Why Does the Torah Start with a Bet?
look.text: The Hebrew Torah begins with the letter bet, the second letter of the alphabet, not aleph, the first. A midrash in Genesis Rabbah notices that the letter bet is closed on three sides and open on the fourth, the side facing the rest of the text. It reads this as a hint: do not ask what is above, below or before creation; ask what comes after.
look.prompt: The midrash takes a fact about a letter's shape and turns it into a lesson. What is the rabbi actually teaching about how to read? Do you find the method convincing?

check.q: What does the word midrash come from?
choices: A word meaning scroll
The name of a town in Babylonia
A root meaning to search or seek
A Greek word for story
check.why: Midrash comes from the root d-r-sh, to search; a midrash is what a reader finds by searching a verse closely.

check.q: What usually starts a midrash?
choices: A dream the rabbi had
A rule from Roman law
A passage from the Septuagint
Something in the text itself: an odd word, a repeated phrase or a gap
check.why: Midrash grows out of details in the verse; it is a response to the text, not free invention.

check.q: Which describes midrash aggadah?
choices: Stories and explanations that seek meaning in a verse
Rules about how to keep Shabbat
The vowel points added by the Masoretes
The Aramaic translation of the Torah
check.why: Aggadah is the story-and-meaning side of rabbinic teaching; midrash halakhah draws law from the text.

lessons.title: Abraham and the Idols
lessons.mainIdea: The famous story of young Abraham smashing his father's idols is not in the Torah; it is a midrash that answers the question of why God chose him.
reading: Ask many people to tell a story about Abraham, and they will tell this one. Young Abraham is left in charge of his father's idol shop. He smashes all the idols but the biggest one and puts a stick in its hand. When his father comes back, Abraham says the big idol did it. His father says idols cannot do anything. "Then why do you worship them?" Abraham asks.

Here is the surprise: that story is not in the Tanakh. Open Genesis 12 and you find God telling Abram to leave his land, with no reason given. The Torah says nothing about idols, a shop or a stick. The story comes from *Genesis Rabbah*, a collection of midrash edited about a thousand years after the events it describes.

So what gap is it filling? The rabbis asked why God spoke to Abraham and not to someone else. The Torah does not say. The midrash answers: because Abraham had already figured out, on his own, that idols were empty. It also builds on a hint in the text. Joshua 24:2 says Abraham's father, Terah, served other gods.

The story has traveled far. A version of it appears in the Qur'an, where the prophet Ibrahim breaks the idols and blames the largest. Jewish and Muslim readers each tell it in their own way. For a student of the Tanakh, the lesson is to know which stories are in the text and which come from its readers.

words.d: a large collection of midrash on Genesis, edited in the land of Israel around the 5th century CE
Abraham's father; the Torah says he took the family from Ur toward Canaan, and Joshua 24:2 says he served other gods

look.title: What the Torah Actually Says
look.text: The Torah says that the LORD told Abram to go out from his country, from his birthplace and from his father's house, to a land that God would show him. God promises to make him a great nation and to bless him. Abram goes. No reason for the choice is given.
look.cite: Genesis 12:1–4, paraphrased from the JPS Tanakh (1917)
look.prompt: List what the Torah leaves out here. Which of those gaps does the midrash about the idols fill, and what does it leave alone?

check.q: Where does the story of Abraham smashing the idols come from?
choices: Genesis chapter 12
A midrash in Genesis Rabbah, not the Torah
The book of Joshua
The Masoretic notes
check.why: The Torah gives no reason for God's call to Abram; the idol story is a rabbinic midrash that fills that gap.

check.q: Which verse gives the midrash a hint to build on?
choices: Genesis 1:1, which says God created the heaven and the earth
Psalm 23, about the shepherd
Joshua 24:2, which says Terah served other gods
Exodus 20, the Ten Sayings
check.why: Joshua 24:2 mentions that Abraham's father served other gods, and the midrash grows from that detail.

check.q: What question is the idol story answering?
choices: How old Abraham was when he left Ur
Where the land of Canaan is
Why the Torah begins with the letter bet
Why God chose Abraham and not someone else
check.why: The Torah does not say why Abraham was chosen; the midrash answers that he had already rejected idols on his own.

lessons.title: Many Answers, One Verse
lessons.mainIdea: The rabbis often preserved several conflicting midrashim on one verse, treating the text as rich enough to carry more than one meaning.
reading: A modern reader might expect a commentary to give one right answer. Rabbinic midrash does not work that way. On a single verse, Genesis Rabbah may give the views of three or four rabbis, one after another, with "another interpretation" between them. None is marked as the winner.

The rabbis had a picture for this. The Talmud compares a verse to a rock struck by a hammer: one blow, many sparks. A verse, they said, can carry many meanings at once. That did not mean anything goes. Each reading had to grow from the words and fit the rest of the Torah.

This habit shaped Jewish reading for good. Later commentators quote midrash freely, choose among midrashim, or reject one and explain why. A reader of Rashi learns to ask which midrash he picked and what problem in the verse it solved. The text stays open, and every generation adds to the conversation.

Historians see something else in the many-answers habit. It let a tradition change while feeling continuous. A new question could be answered from an old verse, and the answer took its place beside older ones. That is one reason the Tanakh has stayed alive for its readers across so many centuries.

words.d: an explanation of what a text means; the rabbis often preserved several for one verse
the great collection of rabbinic discussion built on the Mishnah, edited about 500 CE in Babylonia

look.title: One Blow, Many Sparks
look.text: The rabbis of the Talmud read Jeremiah's line that God's word is like a hammer that shatters rock. Just as a hammer blow scatters many sparks, they taught, one verse of Scripture can yield many meanings.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 34a, on Jeremiah 23:29; paraphrased
look.prompt: What are the limits of this idea? If a verse can mean many things, how would a rabbi decide that a reading is wrong?

check.q: How does Genesis Rabbah usually handle a verse with several possible meanings?
choices: It gives several rabbis' readings one after another without naming a winner
It picks one reading and deletes the rest
It leaves the verse without any comment
It translates the verse into Greek
check.why: Midrash collections string readings together with "another interpretation," keeping more than one view on the page.

check.q: What does the hammer-and-sparks image teach?
choices: The Torah must be written on stone
One verse can carry many meanings
Only one reading of a verse is ever right
Scribes must strike the parchment to flatten it
check.why: The Talmud (Sanhedrin 34a) uses Jeremiah's hammer to say a single verse scatters many meanings, like sparks.

check.q: Which of these is a limit on midrash, according to the reading?
choices: A reading must come from Greek philosophy
A reading must agree with Rashi
A reading must grow from the words and fit the rest of the Torah
A reading must be less than one sentence long
check.why: Many readings are allowed, but each has to be rooted in the text and consistent with the Torah as a whole.

lessons.title: Peshat and Derash
lessons.mainIdea: Peshat is the plain sense of a verse in its context; derash is the meaning a reader searches out beyond it; Jewish tradition values both.
reading: Jewish readers have long spoken of levels in a text. The first is *peshat*, the plain sense. What do the words mean in their context, in ordinary Hebrew, in this story? If Genesis says Jacob wrestled with a man until dawn, the peshat asks who that man is in the story and what the fight is about.

The second is *derash*, the searched-out meaning. This is the level of midrash. It asks what more the words can hold. Why does the text say "a man" and not name him? Why until dawn? A derash might read the wrestler as an angel, or as Esau's guardian, or as Jacob's own fear.

The Talmud sets a rule: a verse never loses its plain sense. Whatever else a reader finds, the peshat still stands. The medieval commentators took that rule seriously. Rashi's grandson Rashbam, in the 12th century, wrote that his grandfather admitted he would have written his commentary differently, with more attention to peshat, if he had had time.

Neither level is treated as the enemy of the other. A good reader in this tradition moves between them. First get the plain sense right. Then ask what the tradition has heard in it. A student who skips the peshat may build a tower on sand. A student who stops at the peshat may miss what the text has meant to its readers.

words.d: the plain, contextual meaning of a verse
the searched-out meaning; what a reader finds in a verse beyond its plain sense, the level of midrash

look.title: The Same Fight, Two Levels
look.text: Genesis 32 says Jacob was left alone at night and a man wrestled with him until daybreak. At dawn the stranger asks to be let go, and Jacob will not until he is blessed. The stranger gives Jacob the new name Israel, "for thou hast striven with God and with men, and hast prevailed" (JPS 1917). Jacob limps away.
look.prompt: Give one peshat reading: who is the man, in the story as told? Then give one derash reading: what else could the night fight stand for? Which question is each reading answering?

check.q: What is peshat?
choices: A hidden, mystical meaning
The melody for chanting
The Aramaic translation
The plain meaning of a verse in its context
check.why: Peshat is the plain sense: what the words mean in ordinary Hebrew, in this story, in this place.

check.q: Which level of meaning does midrash work on?
choices: Derash, the searched-out meaning
Peshat, the plain meaning
The masorah
The haftarah
check.why: Derash and midrash share a root; midrash is the searching that finds meaning beyond the plain sense.

check.q: What rule does the Talmud set about peshat?
choices: The plain sense must be ignored once a midrash is found
A verse never loses its plain sense, whatever else is read into it
Only rabbis may read the plain sense
The plain sense is always the only meaning
check.why: The Talmud (Shabbat 63a) says a verse does not depart from its plain meaning; derash adds to peshat but does not replace it.

lessons.title: Remez, Sod and the Orchard
lessons.mainIdea: Later Jewish readers named four levels, peshat, remez, derash and sod, whose first letters spell pardes, orchard, and used them to organize different ways of reading.
reading: By the 13th century, some Jewish thinkers had added two more levels to peshat and derash. *Remez* means hint. It is the level where a verse points to an idea beyond its story, the way a parable points to a lesson. *Sod* means secret. It is the level of Jewish mysticism, called Kabbalah, where readers found hidden teachings about God in the words and even the letters.

Put the four together, peshat, remez, derash, sod, and take the first letter of each. They spell *PaRDeS*, a Hebrew word for orchard. The word choice is not an accident. The Talmud tells of four rabbis who entered the pardes, a mystical experience. Only Rabbi Akiva came out unharmed.

That story is a warning as well as an invitation. The rabbis who told it thought deep reading was powerful and a little dangerous. The four-level scheme kept the plain sense as the ground floor. A reader could climb, but was expected to know which floor he was on.

Historians note that the four levels are a medieval system, not something the Tanakh itself describes. Christian readers in the Middle Ages had a similar four-level scheme of their own. The idea that a sacred text has layers was shared across traditions, even when the readings themselves were very different.

words.d: hint; the level of meaning where a verse points to an idea beyond its story
secret; the mystical level of meaning sought by readers of Kabbalah
orchard; the word spelled by the first letters of peshat, remez, derash and sod, the four levels of meaning

look.title: Four Who Entered the Orchard
look.text: The Talmud tells that four sages entered the pardes: Ben Azzai, Ben Zoma, Elisha ben Abuyah and Rabbi Akiva. One looked and died. One looked and was harmed. One cut the young plants, which the tradition reads as leaving the faith. Rabbi Akiva entered in peace and left in peace.
look.prompt: Why might a tradition that prizes deep study also tell a story in which deep study harms three out of four? What kind of reader does the story praise?

check.q: What do the letters of PaRDeS stand for?
choices: Parashah, Rashi, derash, sofer
Psalms, Ruth, Daniel, Song of Songs
Peshat, remez, derash, sod
Peshat, Ramban, derash, Septuagint
check.why: Pardes, orchard, is spelled by the first letters of the four levels: plain sense, hint, searched-out meaning and secret.

check.q: Which level is linked to Jewish mysticism, or Kabbalah?
choices: Peshat
Remez
Derash
Sod
check.why: Sod means secret; it is the level where kabbalistic readers looked for hidden teachings in the text.

check.q: What do historians say about the four-level scheme?
choices: It is a medieval system, not something the Tanakh itself describes
It was written down by Moses
It is found in the Masoretic notes
Only Christians used a four-level scheme
check.why: The PaRDeS scheme appears among Jewish thinkers around the 13th century; medieval Christians had a parallel four-level system of their own.

lessons.title: Rashi of Troyes
lessons.mainIdea: Rashi (1040–1105), a rabbi in northern France, wrote the most widely studied Jewish commentary on the Tanakh, mixing plain sense with chosen midrash.
reading: The best-known Jewish commentator is *Rashi*. The name is short for Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki. He was born in 1040 in Troyes, a town in northern France, and died there in 1105. He studied in the Rhineland, came home, and wrote commentaries on nearly the whole Tanakh and on most of the Talmud. Tradition says he made his living from wine.

Rashi's method is easy to spot. He quotes a word or phrase from the verse, then explains it in a few lines. Often he asks a short question the verse raises and answers it. When a midrash solves the problem, he brings it. When the plain sense is enough, he stays with that. He wrote that he came to give the peshat and the midrash that settles the words of the text.

His comment on Genesis 1:1 is famous. Quoting an earlier rabbi, he asks why the Torah begins with creation instead of with the first law given to Israel, in Exodus 12. His answer is that the story of creation shows that the whole earth belongs to God, who may give a land to whom He chooses. Readers have argued about that comment for nine hundred years.

Rashi's commentary became the standard first companion to the Torah in Jewish study. It was the first dated Hebrew book ever printed, in 1475 in Italy. Ever since, it has been printed beside the text in a special typeface called Rashi script. A Jewish child learning Torah has usually learned Rashi at the same time.

words.d: Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040–1105) of Troyes, France; author of the most studied Jewish commentary on the Tanakh and Talmud
a written explanation of a text, usually going verse by verse

look.title: Rashi's First Question
look.text: On the first words of Genesis, Rashi cites Rabbi Isaac's question: since the Torah is a book of teaching, why does it not begin with the first commandment given to Israel, in Exodus 12? His answer: the Torah opens with creation so that if the nations say Israel took its land by force, Israel can answer that the earth is God's, and He gives it to whom He sees fit.
look.cite: Rashi on Genesis 1:1, citing Rabbi Isaac; paraphrased
look.prompt: What does this comment assume about the purpose of the Torah? How does Rashi turn a question about order into a claim about meaning?

check.q: Where and when did Rashi live?
choices: Tiberias, about 930
Troyes, France, 1040–1105
Cairo, 1008
check.why: Rashi, Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, was born and died in Troyes in northern France, in the 11th century.

check.q: How does Rashi usually work through a verse?
choices: He rewrites the verse in Aramaic
He counts the letters and words
He quotes a phrase, raises a question it prompts, and answers with plain sense or a chosen midrash
He gives a mystical secret for each letter
check.why: Rashi's short, verse-by-verse comments explain a phrase, often by choosing the midrash that best fits the words.

check.q: Why is Rashi's commentary important in the history of printing?
choices: It was the first book printed by Gutenberg
It was printed on parchment scrolls
It was never printed until 1900
It was the first dated Hebrew book printed, in 1475
check.why: Rashi's Torah commentary was printed in Reggio di Calabria, Italy, in 1475, the first dated Hebrew printed book.

lessons.title: The Page That Argues
lessons.mainIdea: The Mikraot Gedolot page prints the verse with Targum and several commentators around it, and the Talmud's habit of citing verses shows how the rabbis anchored every idea in Scripture.
reading: In 1517 a Christian printer in Venice named Daniel Bomberg published a Hebrew Bible with commentaries around the text. A second, fuller edition came out in 1525. A Jewish scholar named Jacob ben Hayyim edited it. This *Mikraot Gedolot*, the Great Scriptures, set the pattern. It is the page you saw at the start of this chapter.

The layout is a conversation across time. The verse sits in the center. The Targum runs beside it. Rashi takes one margin. Around and below come *Ibn Ezra*, a 12th-century Spanish grammarian who often reads for the plain sense and pokes at Rashi; *Ramban*, a 13th-century Spanish rabbi who argues with both; and others. The reader watches them disagree.

The Talmud shows the older root of this habit. Rabbis in the Talmud rarely state an idea without a verse. They say "as it is said" or "as it is written" and quote the Tanakh. Sometimes the verse plainly supports the point. Sometimes the connection is a clever reading of one word. Either way, the verse is the anchor.

For a student, the page teaches a skill. Read the verse. Read Rashi's question. See how Ibn Ezra answers it differently. Ask who is reading for peshat and who for derash. In Jewish study this is often done in pairs, a *chavruta*, two students reading and arguing together. The page is built for that.

lessons.title: Arguing Is Respect
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish tradition treats careful argument with and about the text as a form of honoring it, from Abraham questioning God to the rabbis ruling that the Torah is not in heaven.
reading: In many settings, arguing with a sacred text sounds like disrespect. In Jewish tradition it is often the opposite. The pattern starts inside the Tanakh. In Genesis 18, Abraham hears that Sodom will be destroyed and pushes back. He asks whether the Judge of all the earth will not do justly, and bargains down from fifty righteous people to ten. The text does not scold him.

The rabbis made argument a method. Pirkei Avot, a collection of rabbinic sayings, teaches that an argument for the sake of Heaven will last. Its example is Hillel and Shammai, two teachers whose schools disagreed for generations. The Talmud records both sides of hundreds of debates. Often it keeps the losing view too.

The most famous story is about an oven. In the Talmud, Rabbi Eliezer argues a point of law against all the other sages. He calls on miracles, and even a voice from heaven agrees with him. Rabbi Joshua answers with a verse from Deuteronomy: the Torah is not in heaven. The sages rule by majority. The story ends with God, as the rabbis tell it, laughing and saying, "My children have defeated Me."

Historians read the oven story as the rabbis claiming that interpretation belongs to the community of readers, not to miracles. Jewish tradition reads it as a teaching about how the Torah lives in study. Either way, the lesson for this chapter is the same. To question a verse closely, and to argue about it with care, is to take it seriously. That is how the Tanakh has been read for two thousand years.

two rabbinic teachers of about the 1st century BCE whose schools famously disagreed; tradition honors their debates

choices: He was a Masorete in Tiberias who added the vowels

review.why: Rashi (1040–1105) of Troyes wrote the standard Jewish commentary; the Masoretes, the Septuagint and Bomberg are different people and times.

choices: The verse itself, with Targum and commentators around it
Rashi's commentary, with the verse in the margin
The masorah notes
A map of Israel
review.why: The biblical text is in the middle in large type; Targum, Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Ramban and others surround it.

review.q: What point does the Talmud's story of the oven make about interpreting Torah?

Interpretation is decided by the majority of the sages, not by voices from heaven
Only Rabbi Eliezer may interpret the Torah
The Torah should not be studied
